Glenda Beal’s roots in lobstering run nearly as deep as her roots in the town that shares her name: Beals Island, Maine. Her husband and two sons are lobstermen, as were her father and uncle, both grandfathers and a few generations before that.
“Our economy runs on lobster fishing, predominantly,” said Beal, 60, a descendant of one of the island’s original settlers.
It’s a tough industry in which to make a living, Beal said, and the three salmon farming operations in nearby Eastern Bay only make it tougher. She said her community’s lobstermen have noticed barren and polluted waters, damaged gear, floating trash and, on one occasion, dead salmon washed up on their shorelines, and they believe aquaculture is to blame.
The corporation that owns these operations, Cooke Aquaculture, a Canadian multinational based in Saint John, New Brunswick, is being sued for business practices alleged to harm the environment, local fisheries and tourism.
“Having areas taken up by [a] large acreage of pens prevents fishermen from fishing in these traditional waters that they’ve always been able to use,” Beal said. “There isn’t a fisherman out there that likes it.”
That’s why Beals Island and a few other Maine towns have recently tried to exert more local control over whether and how aquaculture facilities operate in their waters.
The Growing Industry
Maine’s aquaculture industry contributed more than $200 million to the state’s economy in 2023, according to the Maine Aquaculture Association.
The largest company is Cooke Aquaculture, which has 24 active lease sites along Maine’s coastline, plus inland hatcheries and a processing facility, according to records on the state’s Department of Marine Resources website.
Cooke operates in 16 countries. Its Maine facilities primarily grow Atlantic salmon in open net pens, floating cages within a larger body of water. Each lease site has multiple pens that hold tens of thousands of salmon during their growth from juvenile to adult size.
The company’s net-pen facilities dot sheltered bays along the Maine coast, places that also sustain ecosystems of lobster, periwinkles, oysters, clams and juvenile fish, including the endangered wild Atlantic salmon. Many of those species form the basis for Maine’s commercial fisheries.
According to state regulations, aquaculture sites aren’t allowed to harm these sensitive ecosystems or interfere with active fisheries. Yet, Beal said that’s exactly what she sees happening. The Conservation Law Foundation agrees—and filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine in January 2025 alleging ongoing Clean Water Act violations at Cooke facilities and harm to area fishing and tourism.
Dead in the Water
The daily upkeep of salmon aquaculture—feedings, pen maintenance, treatments for disease and pests when needed—all occurs in the open water and influences the ecosystem far beyond the pen’s boundaries.
Beal said local fishers have reported that former harvest sites near the pens are no longer viable and the seabed is unusually empty of life.
Waste from the pens, including excess food, excrement and sometimes bits of dead fish, rots and can upset the balance of nutrients like nitrogen and sulfide, Beal said. The resulting low-oxygen conditions suffocate life on the seabed below, including the eelgrass beds that protect young fish and crustaceans.
“That’s the nursery bed of all our sea creatures,” Beal said. “They are critically important.”
The CLF lawsuit against Cooke described a “thick layer of toxic sediment on the ocean floor” and a “foul-smelling black sludge” on lobster traps near the net-pen sites.
According to the CLF, Cooke has repeatedly reported toxic sulfide levels at multiple sites. The lawsuit also alleges the company has failed to meet state monitoring requirements on several occasions, exceeded pollutant discharge limits and reported sediment samples “indicative of poor ecological quality.”
Salmon aquaculture formerly used chemicals to treat sea lice in the pens, which were toxic to other marine life. Today, Maine Aquaculture Association Executive Director Sebastian Belle said the industry instead relies on hot-water baths to kill the lice and letting sites fallow to stop disease and parasite spread.
The CLF lawsuit, however, claims that Cooke boats have been witnessed dumping water with blood and a “chemical odor” after delousing activity.
Cooke facilities had major die-offs of their stock at one Maine site in 2021 and two others in 2024. Disease or pests can cause these mass deaths to occur, as can high temperatures or low oxygen.
Beal said dead salmon floated in the water and washed up on beaches around Beals Island after the 2024 die-off. Though the state cleared Cooke of wrongdoing, Beal said there was “very little satisfactory explanation” about what happened, and she believes pollution from the pens played a role.
Past Infractions
Cooke has received six letters of warning and 20 notices of violation from the Maine Department of Environmental Protection in the past decade, as well as a 2019 consent agreement to pay $190,000 in fines for improper sulfide sampling and exceeding the allowed number of fish per pen.
The company has previously been sanctioned in Chile and fined in Canada and Washington state for other violations. Cooke was accused of animal rights abuses and neglecting sanitary standards at Maine facilities in 2019 and again earlier this year.
The latest undercover video, published in May by an animal rights group, prompted state and third-party investigations.
Cooke did not respond to interview requests, but it previously put out a statement declaring that the CLF’s claims are false. Cooke has also filed a motion to dismiss the suit, which is currently awaiting a judicial decision.
Belle and the Maine Aquaculture Association have also repeatedly called the lawsuit’s claims false and misleading. Belle asserted that modern management practices have reduced the input of excess feed, antibiotics

NEW YORK—From the podium of the United Nations General Assembly, Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino called on fellow leaders to support a treaty affirming that nature has inherent rights.
“Today I am announcing that Panama will lead internationally an effort to recognize the universal rights of nature. And I ask all of you to support us in this initiative,” Mulino said.
Panama’s center-right government is working within the longstanding U.N. Harmony with Nature program, proposing language in the triennial Harmony with Nature resolution that would formally open inter-governmental negotiations on a non-binding declaration asserting that nature has rights and articulating what those rights are.
If the resolution passes in December, two co-facilitators—one from a developed country and one from a developing country—would guide governments through drafting and negotiation, with Panama aiming for a proposal by 2030, according to Callie Veelenturf, a marine conservation biologist whose foundation forNature is supporting the initiative.
The contents of any declaration would depend on what is politically feasible. But the 2010 Universal Declaration on the Rights of Mother Earth, produced by thousands of Indigenous peoples, social movement leaders and environmentalists, provides a starting point. So too do hundreds of rights of nature declarations and laws that have proliferated across the world since about 2006.
Panama is one of more than a dozen countries—along with Spain, Ecuador, Bangladesh and New Zealand—that have national laws or court rulings recognizing the legal rights of nature as a whole, or specific ecosystems or species.
Those laws do not say that nature has the same rights as human beings. Rather, they tend to draw heavily on ecological science, articulating what a species or ecosystem needs to survive and have its biological needs met.
Panama’s sea turtle rights law, for example, recognizes the migratory species’ right to “free passage in a healthy environment.” Veelenturf, a leading sea turtle biologist, advised lawmakers on that 2023 legislation as well as on Panama’s earlier rights of nature law, passed in 2022.
Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, frames his country’s pitch to the world as a pragmatic, values-driven model blending science, ethics and hard-nosed enforcement.
In his view, moving to protect nature is both logical and a moral imperative: “It’s not only a rational decision based on science—for me, it is also a personal decision based on ethics and based on what’s the right thing to do.”
Human-caused global environmental crises, from climate change to the extinction risk an estimated 1 million species face, have outpaced governments’ actions to address them. Navarro pointed to flaws in the way many existing laws are designed, including the treaty system that forms the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change. In general, decisions can only be taken when there is consensus, allowing major polluters to block more stringent action. Panama has proposed reforms to allow a simple majority, as the U.N. General Assembly does.
Navarro also criticized the lack of progress at global climate and biodiversity conferences more broadly.
“Please, let’s tell the truth to ourselves, let’s speak the truth to our own citizens—climate negotiations are not going anywhere,” Navarro said. “We continue to have destruction at a massive scale.”
Rights of nature laws, in the view of both its advocates and opponents, upend existing legal systems. Rather than designing environmental protection laws through the lens of human interest, the movement’s aim is to align human-made laws with the biophysical laws of the planet—human activity would need to conform to what science shows species and ecosystems need to thrive.
When Veelenturf approached Panama lawmakers about the rights of nature back in 2020, she led with scientific arguments.
“I brought it from a perspective of nature and nature’s needs,” she said. “I was using data in certain environmental crises in Panama and in the world to represent the threats nature is facing and how rights of nature could be the solution.”
Panama is “proof of concept” for the global push, having demonstrated that it’s possible to enforce nature’s rights while growing the economy, Navarro said.

The country has paired financial momentum with an aggressive environmental agenda: expanding national parks, designating new wetlands of international importance, scaling park rangers from roughly 100 to 700 in two years and deploying high-tech surveillance to curb illegal fishing.
To ensure its environmental gains endure beyond political cycles, Panama is establishing the “Fondo Panamá Natural,” a public-private trust aimed at guaranteeing long-term, insulated funding for conservation.
The country has faced pushback on some of its environmental efforts.
In 2023, Panama’s Supreme Court struck down a billion-dollar copper mining contract, ruling that the government failed to properly consult local and Indigenous communities and violated the human right to a healthy environment. 14c48e555360.text: Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips Treasury yields are soaring, with the 30-year Treasury bond climbing to its highest level since 2004 Thursday. The selloff in bonds started to accelerate Wednesday after a sizzling early report on the economy in September. The big picture: For the bond market, these moves have been big. Bigly even. On Thursday morning, the 30-year yield rose as high as 5.44%. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note was 5.13%. Wednesday's gain of roughly 0.15 percentage point in the 10-year Treasury yield was the biggest since April 2025, when President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement rocked markets. Flashback: Markets heads remember that it was ructions in the bond market — "They were getting yippy ," the president famously said at the time — that prompted Trump to walk back some of the most extreme tariff policies. Yes, but: This time, the dynamics driving the bond market are more complicated, global and difficult to manage. Treasury yields have been moving higher for months on a combination of stronger-than-expected economic activity coupled with uncomfortably high inflation. The surge in data center-related borrowing in the bond market is also pushing up interest rates, as tech borrowers compete with the U.S. Treasury for investor dollars. Case in point: The big driver of Wednesday's surge in yields — which means, remember, that bond prices were falling — was one of the earliest economic reports on the U.S. economy in September. These surveys of corporate purchasing managers suggested booming business in both the U.S. manufacturing and services industries. (JPMorgan economists said they were consistent with a 5% annual run rate for GDP growth.) But they also showed that the prices these companies were paying were soaring as well. (In other words, more inflationary pressures are in the pipeline.) Zoom out: Inflation is anathema for bond market investors as it erodes the value of the interest payments bondholders collect, making them less attractive assets. The September survey data kicked off a wave of selling of Treasurys that rippled through the financial markets. In the money markets — essentially very short-term bond markets — traders began to price in rising odds that Fed will have to pursue a serious cycle of rate hikes to get inflation under control. The markets are now putting more than 50% odds on quarter-point increases at the Fed's October and December meeting. Between the lines: Lurking in the background of the inflation-driven market move is the specter of a U.S. diesel export ban, which the Trump administration is reportedly considering . But there's deep uncertainty about what such a ban would mean for overall inflation. Some industry voices warn that such a ban could actually push prices of other refined products, like gasoline, sharply higher because of the way refineries operate. What they're saying: "The proposed U.S. diesel export ban will not play out as the U.S. administration expects," wrote Susan Bell, an oil analyst with the consulting firm Rystad Energy. "While it may temporarily lower domestic diesel prices, it will cause the prices for all other refined products to soar as U.S. refineries cut run rates to balance their diesel production with the domestic demand." "There is little flexibility to minimize diesel yield without cutting overall refinery throughput," Bell said. The bottom line: The inflationary pressures appear to be building in the economy, which will be a headache both for politicians in the final stretch of the midterm elections and for policymakers like Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh.

A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said.
Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army".
He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented.
Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months.
It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries.
In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.
Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation.
Proxies are often used to carry out the attacks and Russia always denies involvement, despite growing evidence to the contrary.
The fire at the state-owned Polish satellite station broke out on Wednesday night in Wola Krobowska. It remains operational.
The deputy prime minister said it transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.
Asked about the incident at a news conference with Bulgaria's leader on Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he disliked "labelling something as sabotage versus an accident without 100% certainty, but it looks bad".
On Wednesday Poland also said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing it to scramble fighter jets.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states.
Earlier this month, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said it was Europe speaking about preparing for war, adding: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short."
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014.
In Ukraine, Kharkiv and Kyiv experienced the worst of Russia's attacks overnight into Thursday.
In Kharkiv, six people were killed and twelve others injured in a Russian strike on a farm in the village of Stara Hnylytsia, Ukraine's state emergency services said.
It said they were agricultural workers sorting vegetables, with the head of the Kharkiv region adding that four were women.
In Kyiv, two people were killed and eight others injured overnight, emergency services said. More than 50 civilian facilities were also damaged in the city, including a maternity building.
The hospital's director said a woman gave birth to a baby boy in a shelter during that attack, adding: "Even on such a terrible night, life goes on."
Russia's defence ministry said it had hit Ukrainian defence facilities, logistics and telecom centres, as well as vessels used by the military.
Moldova's president said four Russian drones crossed into its airspace, with at least one exploding, while Romania's defence ministry said one drone crashed in its territory.
Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine have become more devastating in recent months because of their new jet-powered drones, which are harder to shoot down.
Kyiv is racing to develop low-cost weapons that can counter them as the missiles and fighter jets it has to fight them are too expensive.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, "we need ballistic interceptors to protect lives" and called on the US to help.
He said Putin needed to be stopped from continuing the war and "spreading this evil further", adding: "Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land."
He said Ukraine would seek to target the Russian energy sector over the winter.
The Ukrainian president's comments came as Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev headed to the US to meet Trump administration officials, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Reuters reported, citing two sources.
Russia's Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday there would be no pause in the war.

African elephants use dozens of different medicinal plants to treat themselves and their families when they are sick.
This is the conclusion of a study which interviewed people who live and work alongside the elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya.
These particular animals have long intrigued scientists with their extraordinary behaviour - they are known as salt-mining elephants, because they go into caves and scrape the rock with their tusks to extract minerals for their diet.
This newly published research suggests that the same elephants use several different plant species in the forest for medicinal purposes.
One of the lead researchers, Dr Elodie Freymann from Brown University in the US, said the study raised the question of whether destruction of forest habitat deprives animals - and humans - of the medicines they need to thrive.
"This shows just how entangled our medicines are with the non-human world," Dr Freymann told BBC News.
Medicine for baby elephants
The scientists collaborated with the conservation charity the Mount Elgon Foundation, external. They interviewed local people, including wildlife scouts and community elders.
Accounts described elephants selecting particular plants when they seemed unwell, and mothers reportedly giving medicinal plant material to their calves.
From this, the researchers concluded that the elephants use 35 different plant species, and that 25 of those are known locally to have medicinal uses.
The study, published in the journal Scientific Reports, external, did not name the interviewees - keeping participants anonymous so they felt free to share their stories.
Their accounts reveal some intriguing details. In one testimony, a wildlife scout described seeing elephants using a plant known as Angurweet "as medicine to give to babies".
Angurweet is used as a remedy for ailments including stomach ache. The scout, who described elephant mothers mixing it in their mouths - "removing the leaves and chewing it until smooth, along with the roots of some other trees".
He also recounted that he had seen mothers mix this plant material with their own milk. "They give it to the babies, who chew on it themselves and spit out the solids".
Professor Michael Huffman, a primatologist based in Japan, currently at Nagasaki University, said this particular account was "tantalising", but more evidence would be needed to prove that elephants provided bespoke medical treatment for their calves.
The scientists have already embarked on gathering that evidence - giving the local wildlife experts they worked with cameras to record the behaviour they witness.
They are also analysing plants that the elephants use - looking for new medicines that the elephants themselves may have discovered.
Another lead reearcher on the project, Dr Fabien Schultz from the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg, told BBC News: "Local knowledge has given us a map".
"We [now] want to follow the elephants and investigate whether they select particular plants in particular health contexts, and whether those plants have relevant biological activity."
Natural medicine factories
Many animals treat themselves with plants and other natural remedies.
The earliest scientific accounts of elephants practicing "self-medication" date back to the early third century.
Roman author Claudius Aelian in his text De Natura Animalium (On the Nature of Animals) described an elephant that, after being wounded by spears and arrows, consumed flowers and oil from an olive tree. The elephant made a full recovery.
Centuries later, these scientists are delving into what we can learn from wildlife about the properties of plants in the forest habitats they evolved in.
"There are medicine-producing organisms on this planet that have this incredible capability," Dr Freymann told BBC News." Medicine factories that exist all around us."
Prof Huffman, who was not involved in this study, added: "We now know that mosquitoes and drosophila (flies) self-medicate, bees self-medicate, as do many other species all the way up the evolutionary ladder to the great apes of Africa and Asia.
"WIth each new species studied, we have gained a greater understanding of our medicinal past."
For Dr Freymann, the findings also contain a lesson for our future.
"So many of the medicines we buy in a pharmacy were derived from compounds from trees, algae, from fungi, from coral reefs.
"It's a win-win for us to protect these forests and keep those natural pharmacies around... long enough that we can discover new natural products that could save us down the line."

A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to immediately reinstate access to the White House for three news organisations barred from the building last week by the president.
A District of Columbia court issued a temporary restraining order against the ban, meaning CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored for 14 days, after ruling the move "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".
The three outlets launched a legal challenge after their reporters had their passes for the White House confiscated and were denied access.
The Trump administration defended the move in court, accusing the outlets of publishing false information and threatening national security - an argument the court rejected.
The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may take further legal action.
Judge Timothy Kelly ruled, external CNN, Politico and MS NOW were "likely to succeed" in showing the White House had not exercised "adequate due process" in implementing the ban.
He also cast doubt on the Trump administration's arguments that the bans were motivated by national security concerns, pointing out the president made no mention of that in his initial announcement.
When President Donald Trump announced the ban on Friday, he accused the three news outlets of writing "fake news" and "fictions and lies" in their coverage of him and his team.
The ruling continued: "The record lacks factual support for Defendants' contention that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the Court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds."
In its defence of the ban in a court filing on Tuesday, the Trump administration cited a number of articles published by the outlets, including some about construction at the White House, including work on a new ballroom.
The judge said that "in most cases" the stories the White House took issue with were written by journalists who "did not even hold card passes" - and in the remaining cases, the Trump administration did not demonstrate "reason to believe that the reporter's possession of the hard pass was integral to the stories identified".
In its original filing, the Trump administration cited declarations from defence department officials supporting the ban - but the judge said they had "no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House, or about any of the facts at issue here".
Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, told CNN, external: "This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law."
On Monday, major US TV networks pulled out of White House pool duties in protest at the ban. The arrangement sees media organisations share material with each other to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public.
Forty-nine media organisations - including CBS News, The New York Times and Fox News - also filed a legal brief in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico's lawsuit.
Trump frequently criticises news organisations, and his administration has launched legal action against a series of outlets, including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the BBC.
Some of the lawsuits have resulted in media organisations agreeing to pay multi-million-dollar settlements. Trump's lawsuit against the BBC is ongoing.

India's Election Commission (ECI) is facing yet another crisis of credibility after a series of fresh allegations of irregularities against its chief.
One of the most trusted public institutions in the world's largest democracy, the three-member commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and includes Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as commissioners.
The latest row broke out after a report in the Indian Express newspaper, external said that in the past few months, CEC Kumar had been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database, changes to the way new voters are enrolled and the security of the electoral rolls itself.
The report said that Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi objected to several decisions which were taken without their knowledge. There were at least 14 times in the past 10 months when Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi were kept in the dark, it added.
In one instance, the report says, the two commissioners even wrote a letter complaining to the chief secretary, the top bureaucrat in the Indian government.
The revelations have created a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. Sandhu and Joshi have not publicly commented on the report but the ECI said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process".
The report comes at a time when the commission is carrying out a controversial country-wide revision of the electoral database.
The Election Commission says the aim of this Special Intensive Revision - better known by its acronym SIR - is to ensure that no ineligible name remains on the rolls.
It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address.
But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing CEC Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
But the latest revelations are being seen as much more serious as they are about questions being raised from within the Election Commission about the way its chief is functioning.
From the start, questions have lingered over the robustness of the revision, which has seen 130 million names from across India struck off the voters' list.
Millions of voters have also complained to the authorities that their names are missing, saying the new process set by SIR to register as voters is too cumbersome and involves furnishing documents that many don't have.
Former CEC SY Quraishi, who says he has "been a critic of the SIR from the beginning", told news agency PTI that he always wondered why Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had been "keeping quiet".
"[Now] I realised that very silently and quietly they were protesting, they were writing notes. That is a good thing, they have gone up in my esteem," he said.
The revelations have also provided fresh ammunition to the opposition parties and critics who have repeatedly claimed that SIR is being used to exclude their voters for the BJP's benefit and that elections in India are no longer free and fair.
On Wednesday, angry opposition politicians once again questioned the sanctity of India's election process and demanded that CEC Kumar resign, saying he had no right to continue in office, with some even calling for his arrest.
The charge was led by MP and senior Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi who has repeatedly accused the Commission of "stealing votes from the opposition". On Wednesday, he also accused the Commission and its officers of "treason".
"Vote chori [theft] is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution. The BJP, RSS [Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh] and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served," he posted on X, external. He also shared a 15-second video telling the commission and its officers that "your time will come. You cannot get away".
Mamata Banerjee, leader of the regional Mamata All India Trinamool Congress, called for Kumar's arrest and demanded fresh polls with the pre-SIR voters' list in the state of West Bengal which she lost to the BJP in the recent elections. At least 2.7million voters were removed in the state during SIR - Banerjee and her supporters say that cost them dozens of seats and the election win.
Within hours of the Indian Express report and statements from opposition leaders, the Election Commission put out a statement, external defending its way of working.
"Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken.
"Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the statement said.
The note said that highlighting "certain specific internal notes and observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives" give only part of the picture.
And that in recent months, the commission has "introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full commission in the past one year".
The BJP has also defended CEC Kumar, calling the opposition criticism a "smear campaign" and that dissent was "a sign of a vibrant democracy".
Party spokesperson Sambit Patra told a press conference that "ever since the Modi government came to power in 2014, opposition parties have been collapsing one after the other". And because they cannot win

Nene Royal, a 16-year-old rocker, has been crowned the latest winner of America's Got Talent - making her the first ever Thai winner of the long-running talent show.
For the show's finals on Tuesday in California, Nene, whose real name is Rattikarn Amloy, performed a rendition of Seven Nation Army by American rock duo The White Stripes.
Her heavy metal performances trumped nine other finalists, including magician acts, canine performers and even a robot dance crew.
Many in Thailand are celebrating her win, with some saying they were proud that she had made it to "one of the biggest stages in the world". The Thai government has called her an "inspiration to anyone who dares to dream big".
Nene emerged as a clear fan favourite early in the competition, after a viral clip of her audition, in which she belted out Zombie by The Cranberries to a stunned panel of judges. The video has racked up 20 million views.
On Wednesday night, ahead of the results being announced, Nene took the stage with Linkin Park to perform The Emptiness Machine, a 2024 rock song by the American band.
Later that night she broke down in tears, kneeling on the ground as she was crowned the winner of the show's 21st season - which comes with a prize of $1m (Â£755,000).
"I'm very happy and emotional right now," she said, thanking everyone for supporting her.
The results show was also eagerly followed by her legion of fans in Thailand, who were unable to watch the live broadcast on the television network NBC.
Many in Thailand had to resort to a YouTube livestream instead - and were thrown into distress when the livestream was abruptly cut in the middle of the results announcements.
But moments later came sighs of relief and exclamations of joy, as word got around that Nene had secured her historic victory.
"History made!" one Thai social media user wrote on Facebook.
"Let the world write it down that this Thai kid is incredibly talented," wrote another.
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul congratulated Nene Royal, saying in a statement that she had "brought honour to Thailand" and "instilled pride in the Thai people" with her win.
"What makes this win special is that Nene carried her Thai identity with confidence onto one of the world's biggest stages," the Thai government's public relations department said in another statement on Thursday.
"She showed that talent, hard work, and determination can come from anywhere, including a young girl from Phuket with a guitar and a big dream."
According to Nene, she started playing the guitar when she was seven years old and harboured dreams of becoming a touring musician.
In her hometown of Phuket, a tourist hub known for its beaches and seaside resorts, Nene was known to busk at Naka Weekend Market.
Piyarat Na Songkhla, 43, tour guide in Phuket, tells the BBC that he has seen Nene Royal perform since she was young.
"She's so adorable," he says. "I feel so elated and happy for her. It's unbelievable that she has gone this far. So proud of her."
The Facebook account of Naka Weekend Market posted a tribute to Nene after her victory.
"Everyone at Naka Market is so proud to see you shine on one of the biggest stages in the world," its post reads.
"Your talent, heart, and courage have inspired so many people, and this victory is a beautiful reminder of what can happen when someone truly gives everything to their dream."
Kajonkiet International School in Phuket, where Nene studies, also congratulated her on the win.
"We are so proud of you," reads a Facebook post from the school, which posted a video of its students and staff gathering to watch Nene's final performance, screaming and chanting her name.

Southeast Asian countries are continuing a $160 billion gas buildout, even as the Middle East conflict exposed the import-dependent regionâs vulnerability to supply shocks and high prices. Analysis by Global Energy Monitor shows more than 100 gigawatts of gas power and 70 million tonnes per year of LNG import capacity are still being planned across the region. Domestic gas fields could help cushion future shocks, but new supplies take years to develop and wonât remove the regionâs growing exposure to LNG imports, the report found.
Developments in Thailand and Vietnam show early signs of a rethink, however. Thailand plans to reduce its reliance on imported LNG in favor of renewable and nuclear power, while in Vietnam, private conglomerate Vingroup proposed replacing a planned 4.8 GW LNG power plant with renewable generation, citing the risk of high LNG prices. At the same, Wood Mackenzie found the boom in data centers is driving structural demand for LNG in the region, which the new import infrastructure could help meet.

Chinese exports of solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, and EVs prevented 374 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions last year, more than the annual emissions of the UK, new analysis found. The findings from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air show how rapidly falling solar and battery prices are starting to transform energy systems around the world: Solar panel exports to South Asia alone were responsible for almost a third of the avoided emissions.
Chinaâs clean energy manufacturing boom is powering the global energy transition at a time when the US has pulled out of the âbattlefieldâ, former US climate envoy John Kerry told Bloomberg. On Wednesday, as US President Donald Trump prepared to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, the White House argued that an extension to the US-China trade truce, which paused tit-for-tat tariffs above 100% until January, would give the two sides more time to work on a bigger deal.

4e8a1a390f40.text: By — Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press Jocelyn Noveck, Associated Press By — Hallie Golden, Associated Press Hallie Golden, Associated Press By — Laurie Kellman, Associated Press Laurie Kellman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-orders-white-house-to-restore-access-to-cnn-ms-now-and-politico-reporters-say-theyre-still-blocked Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge orders White House to restore access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Reporters say they're still blocked Politics Sep 24, 2026 9:24 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — A federal judge temporarily blocked President Donald Trump's ban of three news outlets from the White House, ordering early Thursday that CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored. Reporters from all three outlets, however, said they remained blocked a few hours after the ruling. The back-and-forth is the latest in an extraordinary showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump first announced he was banning the outlets Friday, assailing what he called "fake news," and only later arguing that their reporting was a risk to national security. The outlets argued in a joint lawsuit that the ban was a blatant violation of the First Amendment because it singled them out for the content of their coverage. In his late-night ruling, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" the three outlets' access. He said they had met the legal thresholds to obtain a temporary restraining order, in effect for 14 days, and were likely to succeed in showing that their press passes were revoked without due process. "This is a high bar, but Plaintiffs have met it," he wrote. Kelly — whom Trump nominated in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist's access restored in a similar case in 2018 — said the government must have clear standards for conduct that would lead to revoking a press pass. He called the standard of objectionable reporting outlined in letters that the White House sent the outlets "so vague it hardly does the trick." The judge also made clear he did not buy the administration's argument that the news outlets' reporting endangered national security — and noted that Trump himself had not used that argument in the beginning, focusing solely on what he called negative coverage. "Nothing in the record ... suggests that the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes was motivated by national security concerns," he wrote. The ruling came after Kelly heard arguments in an emergency hearing Wednesday. Temporary restraining orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court. "This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in an emailed statement. "We greatly appreciate the court's swift action." But a few hours after the ruling, reporters from those outlets said they were not allowed to enter the White House. The White House did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on the order. Attorneys debated access to the White House and any risk to national security Boutrous argued in the hearing that there was an urgent need for renewed access, saying that the ban caused irreparable harm to the outlets at a time of momentous news events. "We're at war. We have world leaders coming to Washington." Justice Department attorney Michael Velchik, in his argument, reiterated the administration's point that the president has the right to choose who gets into the White House. "Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," Velchik said. In arguing that Trump was not engaging in viewpoint discrimination — the government singling out specific media outlets for the content of what they say or publish — Velchik said the president had criticized other news organizations, but not banned them. He noted, for example, that Trump had called ABC "the worst." He added: "The president should be able to take immediate action to protect national security." In response, Boutrous said, "Suddenly it's a national security case," arguing that the president brought up that point only after the lawsuit was filed. Trump "keeps proving our point," Boutrous said, describing how the president has consistently used negative coverage of him as justification for the ban. Kelly seemed to agree, writing of the national security claim: "Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was 'banning' Plaintiffs from the White House — instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of Plaintiffs' reporting." The Trump administration outlined 'reporting incidents' of each news outlet In a filing Tuesday, administration lawyers detailed letters sent to each of the three news outlets that identified "a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents, including those that have threatened national security and spread falsehoods." Among the incidents cited were: CNN reporting on "'top-secret' construction details related to the East Wing bunker"; MS NOW reporting "on an alleged leak investigation"; and Politico publishing "a document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements." Politico's letter also included an incident in June of a report in which a "senior administration official … granted anonymity" predicted whether a preliminary deal would end the conflict with Iran. That item appeared to reference a background briefing set up by the White House, where an official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity

Oil prices rose above $100 a barrel on the US-Iran geopolitical deadlock. Iranâs president said Wednesday he was open to talks to end the war, but warned that Tehran wouldnât surrender its nuclear program â a major sticking point in the negotiations â or âbowâ to the US. Yet, more oil and gas is reported to be moving through the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar has ramped up LNG shipments to the highest levels in over two months and Saudi crude exports are on the rise.

Timâs view
On top of power hardware shortages, angry neighbors, and permitting delays, data center developers have a new headache to deal with: skeptical insurers. Wall Street is more than happy to rain cash down on AI infrastructure. But the insurance industry is still struggling to design and price coverage for these massive, super-expensive buildings, Joe Peiser, CEO of risk capital at Aon, told me Wednesday: âInsurance really is a bottleneck.â
Climate change impacts are one problem: Data centers consume huge volumes of water, leaving them exposed to drought, and many are being planned in places that are prone to floods, fires, tornadoes, or other disasters. Up to 80% of data center projects globally are exposed to such hazards, a recent study from the risk analytics firm First Street found. Investors and insurers are starting to ask developers more pointed questions about the buildingsâ physical integrity and siting, Peiser said, and asking for better forecasts about future climate exposure. Data centers are also expensive, reaching into the tens of billions of dollars; insurers are starting to get sufficient capital in place to cover that volume of risk, but are struggling to keep up with the requirements of the biggest hyperscalers. The tightness of the power equipment supply chain is another major risk. If a gas turbine breaks, and the queue for replacement parts takes weeks or months, âthat loss to insurers or their policyholder or both is going to be dramatically higher than anyone is currently thinking about,â Peiser said.
Usually insurers have a simple way to deal with novel or unknown risks: Just charge more for coverage. In the case of energy infrastructure and oil tankers in the Middle East that were suddenly exposed to missiles and drones this year, for example, insurers adapted quickly rather than walking away. The same story will apply to data centers; theyâre unlikely to become completely uninsurable, even with climate risk. But keeping them covered wonât be cheap. And some critical questions remain unanswered.
If power problems, permitting delays, or extreme weather cause a data center to go offline or drag out its launch date, and a Big Tech companyâs AI business suffers as a result, âhow do you quantify that, and how do insurers respond?â Peiser said. âI foresee that being a significant mess.â
Notable
- AI data center backlash is partly driven by âfear of the unknown,â Nvidiaâs head of sustainability told Semafor at The Next 3 Billion event. He called these fears a âfundamentalâ human response.

Warnings of an El Niño unlike any other are starting to become reality.
For months, scientists have cautioned that the natural climate pattern could grow into a record-breaking beast, releasing extraordinary amounts of heat from the ocean and fueling droughts, floods, heat waves and severe storms. Now, a traditional strength measurement of El Niño, called the Oceanic Niño Index, indicates that the pattern has reached an intensity unseen in recorded history.
On September 21, the daily sea surface temperature in the region where El Niño develops — the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean — reached 3.08 degrees Celsius warmer than the 1991 to 2020 average. That’s more extreme than any other El Niño ever recorded.
Hotter water
Since El Niño emerged in June, the daily average sea surface temperature has climbed extraordinarily high in the heart of the Pacific Ocean region where El Niño develops. On September 21, it reached 3.08 degrees Celsius above both the 1991 to 2020 average (coarse dashed line) and the 1982 to 2010 average (fine dashed line). Prior to this month, the most extreme anomaly on record was 3.02 degrees Celsius, set by an El Niño in November 2015.
“It has been a remarkable event,” says Nathaniel Johnson, a climate scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory in Princeton, N.J. What’s more, the El Niño will probably grow even stronger, Johnson says. “We’re probably going to reach our peak within the next few months.”
The oceanic heat released by the phenomenon could contribute to an increase in global land temperatures of about 1.2 degrees Celsius over the coming months, leading to over 450,000 additional heat-related deaths by February 2027, researchers from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago report.
NOAA has yet to declare this event the strongest on record. It uses a rolling three-month-average anomaly, rather than the daily anomaly, in calculations of an El Niño’s strength. And it’s shifted to a new method for measuring El Niño strength, called the Relative Oceanic Niño index, which better represents the phenomenon’s ability to sway weather globally. By that measurement, the current El Niño has yet to surpass the strength of the one in 1997 and 1998.
But that record is on track to be broken soon, the latest seasonal forecast from NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center suggests. To understand what’s driving this historic El Niño and its potential impact, Science News spoke with Johnson, who is part of the team that produces the forecasts, and Nathan Lenssen, a climate scientist at the National Center of Atmospheric Research in Boulder, Colo. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
SN: How much of this El Niño’s strength has been fueled by human-caused climate change?
Johnson: It’s really an unanswered question. If we look at the historical record, we have been seeing more rapid swings between El Niño and La Niña [which is the other extreme phase of the El Niño Southern Oscillation that generally has the opposite effect on weather patterns]. There’s some evidence from simulations that increasing greenhouse gas emissions leads to more of those extreme swings. But there’s not yet a scientific consensus on how climate change is impacting El Niño, especially an extreme El Niño like this one.
Lenssen: It’s a matter of debate how much we can directly attribute to climate change. But due to the warming of the planet, there is more energy in the oceans now, and El Niños are when the ocean releases some of that heat into the atmosphere.
SN: What are the most predictable and unpredictable impacts of this El Niño?
Johnson: We see a lot of the most predictable impacts in the tropical regions, as that’s where El Niño itself develops. We’ve already seen this suppressed Atlantic hurricane season and enhanced Pacific hurricane season, and we’ve also seen droughts in Central America. We also tend to see droughts over northern South America and the Amazon, and a weakening of the Indian monsoon.
As we get into late fall, we typically see more impacts a little farther from the equator. For instance, over the southern part of the United States we tend to see rainier conditions, whereas it’s typically drier than normal over the Pacific Northwest and warmer than average over the northern United States and Canada.
Lenssen: An important detail is that just because this El Niño is so powerful, that doesn’t necessarily mean we’re more confident about these impacts. The global warming of the oceans has made some of the historical mid-latitude impacts less likely, so there’s a kind of twist there. For example, the El Niño in 2023 and 2024 didn’t lead to as much wet weather in California as expected, and some research has shown that was due to other warming ocean patterns. That clouds the picture a little.
SN: How long could this El Niño last?
Johnson: El Niños typically last just a year, so we’ll probably see it weaken after winter and be over by spring or early summer. But when we have big El Niño like this, we’re more likely to see a shift in the following year to La Niña [which can also have global impacts on weather]. So that’s definitely something we’ll be keeping our eye on.
Lenssen: It’s possible that this event could be followed by a double La Niña, which is when we get back-to-back events separated by a brief period of neutral conditions. That happened in 2016 and 2017, after the strong El Niño of 2014 and 2015.
SN: Aside from its strength, what sets this event apart from others in the past?
Johnson: We’ve seen such a dramatic change in the equatorial Pacific Ocean over the course of the year. The transition has been very rapid, from a La Niña last winter to a very strong El Niño in less than a year. That might be the fastest transition that we’ve seen.

dfc6808f0ecf.text:
Earlier this week, President Donald Trump responded to rising public concerns about artificial intelligence with a post on Truth Social.
“The same people that said, ‘We’ll all be dead in twelve years because of Global Warming,’ a name since ‘reborn’ to Climate Change, because the Planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead, are the people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us, that robots are going to attack us, and everything is a DISASTER,” he wrote on Truth Social.
He then declared fear of AI “a hoax.”
I found it notable that he injected climate denial into the discussion of AI, as if that would help his argument, and that he did so on the first day of Climate Week NYC.
The annual event has included corporations touting how AI could help the climate. For example, the chip maker Nvidia highlighted how its AI products are being used to advance clean energy, such as operational improvements at a nuclear power plant and energy-storage projects that utilize used batteries. Josh Parker, Nvidia’s head of sustainability, expanded on this in an interview Wednesday with The New York Times at Climate Week. He said AI could help reduce emissions reductions for transportation, manufacturing and buildings, with benefits that would outweigh AI’s climate footprint.
Looking at Trump’s comments alongside some of the hopeful messages coming from Climate Week, I see an evolving AI discourse that mixes climate denial and techno-optimism, neither of which is helpful.
Trump was touching on—and dismissing—concerns that AI would lead to superintelligent computers that would kill people. Yes, that’s a reason to worry, but the more immediate concern is AI’s vast need for water, electricity and investor dollars.
So what’s the reality? The most useful encapsulation of the peril and opportunity of this moment, in my view, was the paper published in a Nature journal in August that finds the increase in carbon emissions from powering AI data centers and using AI to help optimize fossil fuel production is much more than the savings from using AI for end uses related to clean energy. (My colleague Arcelia Martin wrote about the paper.)
The co-authors include Will Alpine and Holly Alpine, a couple who worked on AI at Microsoft before starting a nonprofit, the Enabled Emissions Campaign, which calls on technology companies to be accountable for how AI will boost fossil fuel use.
Their paper’s findings align with statements from organizations such as the International Energy Agency, which has said the potential climate benefits from AI-enabled systems are still on the horizon, while some concerning ramifications will come sooner, such as increased electricity demand for data centers.
I asked Holly Alpine what she makes of the talk of AI at Climate Week.
“What we’re seeing at Climate Week is a familiar pattern: companies spotlighting a handful of clean energy pilot projects while the overwhelming majority of AI’s actual applications are aimed at increasing fossil fuel extraction and production,” she said in an email. “Nvidia’s post is a good example—highlighting a renewable energy partnership is easy and photogenic, while conveniently omitting how much AI is being deployed to find, extract, and produce more oil and gas.”
This isn’t complicated. If AI were powered mostly by clean sources and its emissions-cutting uses outweighed its climate-harming uses, then there would be no need to mislead about the effects.
Jonathan Koomey, an independent researcher who has been studying data centers for decades, is wary of companies describing AI as beneficial for the climate while not acknowledging the potential downsides.
I spoke with him recently following a speech he gave in my city, Columbus, Ohio, about the challenges of accurately forecasting the scale of the data center boom— a particularly relevant topic in Columbus, one of the country’s leading data center markets.
“Projecting short-term trends for even 10 or 12 years is a recipe for disaster, in my experience,” he told me.
Koomey’s larger point is that the scale of the data center boom remains uncertain. One of the most harmful scenarios is that utility companies build new power plants to serve anticipated data centers, only for many, if not most, of those projects to never materialize. If that happens, households and businesses would be left to cover the costs through their utility bills. Regulators and lawmakers need to take steps to protect consumers, he said.
For now, one of the most troubling aspects of the AI data center boom is how the rush to build as fast as possible has led developers to rely on some of the least efficient and most expensive power technologies, such as natural gas combustion turbines.
“It’s madness,” Koomey said, noting that many of the turbines are essentially jet engines, built for short-term use. “No sane person would buy electricity from combustion turbines running 24-7. It just wouldn’t happen.”
At some point, economic gravity will assert itself, he said. Data centers will need to recoup their development costs and determine how much customers are willing to pay.

The Emiratesâ largest expat group will soon pay bills the way they did back home. PhonePe, Indiaâs biggest payments app, won approval from the UAE Central Bank to launch in the country, the Walmart-backed companyâs first move abroad. It will offer payments, remittances, and money management to the UAEâs 4.3 million Indian residents.
The UAE fintech industry is projected to nearly double by 2029, after drawing in a third of all startup funding in the country in 2024. The central bank has been licensing digital wallets at a clip, including Careem Pay, e& money, Botim, and buy-now-pay-later firm Tabby. With expatriates making up nearly 90% of the UAEâs population, remittances are a prize worth billions. UAE residents sent India more than $21 billion last year, nearly a fifth of Indiaâs total remittances and second only to the US.
